title: Binary & Bits
tagline: How two symbols — 0 and 1 — encode every number, image, and program you have ever used.

sections.content:
Every photo, song, and program is ultimately a long sequence of 0s and 1s. A single symbol is a **bit** (binary digit) — the smallest unit of information, representing one of two states. String enough together and you can encode anything.

Binary is just the **base-2 number system**. Each position is worth twice the one to its right — identical logic to decimal, only the base changes. Master this and hex, bitwise ops, and low-level debugging stop feeling like dark arts.

sections.caption: One byte — 8 bit positions, each worth double the previous. All 1s = 255.

sections.title: Odometers in Different Bases
sections.content: A decimal odometer has wheels with 10 symbols (0–9). When a wheel passes 9 it resets to 0 and carries into the next wheel. Binary is the same machine but each wheel holds only 2 symbols. It fills up faster: 0, 1, carry → 10 (two), 11 (three), carry → 100 (four). Two-symbol wheels are cheap because a physical switch is either off or on.

**Place value** is everything. In decimal, 305 = 3×10² + 0×10¹ + 5×10⁰. Binary uses powers of 2: positions are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 (right to left). So 1011₂ = 8+0+2+1 = **11**.

To convert decimal → binary, repeatedly subtract the largest fitting power of 2. For 13: 8 fits (5 left), 4 fits (1 left), 2 doesn't, 1 fits → bits **1101**.

Eight bits form a **byte** holding 2⁸ = 256 values (0–255). Four bits (a nibble) map to one hex digit (0–F). Computers use binary because transistors are two-state switches — far cheaper and more noise-tolerant than distinguishing ten voltage levels.

sections.explanation: toString(2) is JS's built-in decimal-to-binary shortcut. The manual fromBinary loop makes place value explicit — it walks bits right-to-left, multiplying each by an increasing power of two.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: Interview trap: '8 bits can hold 256 values' but the maximum value is 255. Confusing the two causes real off-by-one bugs. Also: adding one bit doesn't add one to the range — it doubles it. 8 bits → 256; 9 bits → 512.

items: A bit is one binary digit (0 or 1); 8 bits = 1 byte = 256 distinct values (0–255).
Binary is base-2 positional notation — each position is a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 …).
n bits represent 2ⁿ values; the maximum unsigned value is 2ⁿ − 1; each added bit doubles the range.
Computers use binary because two-state transistor switches are cheap, fast, and noise-tolerant.
One hex digit = exactly 4 bits (a nibble) — hex is a compact shorthand for binary.

quiz.question: What is the decimal value of binary 1011?
How many distinct values can 8 bits represent?
quiz.explanation: 2⁸ = 256 distinct values (0 through 255). 255 is the maximum value, not the count.

quiz.question: What is the place value of the 5th bit position from the right (0-indexed as position 4)?
Why do computers use binary rather than decimal internally?
options: Binary numbers are always shorter than decimal
Two-state switches are cheap and noise-tolerant
Binary stores more values per digit
quiz.explanation: Transistors act as on/off switches. Two clearly separated voltage states are cheap and reliable — distinguishing ten levels would be error-prone.

quiz.question: Adding one bit to a binary number does what to the count of representable values?
quiz.explanation: 2^(n+1) = 2 × 2ⁿ, so each additional bit doubles the count of distinct values.

quiz.question: How many bits map exactly to one hexadecimal digit?
quiz.explanation: Hex digits range 0–15, requiring 4 bits (2⁴ = 16). This 4-bit group is called a nibble.

quiz.question: What is the maximum unsigned integer a single byte can store?
quiz.explanation: A byte holds 256 values (0–255). The maximum is 255 because 0 uses one slot: 2⁸ − 1 = 255.
